priority submetering solutions

Why Priority Submetering Matters for Property Owners Right Now

Utility management has become an operating issue, not a facilities side project. Owners are dealing with volatile expenses, residents who expect understandable charges, insurers who want stronger leak controls, and regulators who scrutinise how consumption is measured and disclosed. A bulk invoice tells you what the building purchased. It doesn't tell you which suite, fixture, common area, or system created the cost.
Ontario provides a useful picture of the scale. A residential bill comparison analysed approximately
170,000 sub-metering customers
and estimated average monthly payments of
$66.52 with sub-metering
, compared with
$78.43 with individual utility metering by the local distribution company
. The estimated difference was
$11.91 per month
, and
94% of customers paid less with sub-metering
in that comparison, as documented in the
Ontario bill comparison analysis
The business case is also behavioural. A University of Toronto study estimated that sub-metering reduced condominium electricity usage by
about 20%
. The same source recorded that
26% of Ontario residents lived in multi-unit buildings
, while
75% to 90% of those buildings used bulk metering
at the time of the study, highlighting how much consumption historically remained shared rather than assigned to individual occupants. Those findings appear in the
Canadian government record of the Ontario condominium sub-metering study
Treat the rollout as an operating intervention

A conventional project waits for capital approval, procurement, contractor availability, and a convenient access window. That approach can be sensible for a low-pressure asset. It fails when delayed billing, unresolved leaks, or an acquisition deadline is already affecting the owner's numbers.
Priority service changes the sequence:
Speed:
The provider organises survey, equipment, crews, commissioning, and billing preparation as one managed programme.
Cost recovery:
The owner moves toward unit-level charges instead of leaving all consumption inside a bulk expense line.
Risk transfer:
The provider takes responsibility for equipment, maintenance, data handling, and billing administration under the service agreement.
Operational visibility:
The owner receives consumption information that can support leak response, budgeting, resident communication, and audit preparation.

The service tier earns its place when the property can justify faster deployment and stronger accountability. If the only objective is to purchase meters at the lowest initial price, standard procurement may be adequate. If the owner needs revenue, control, and compliance without waiting through a long capital cycle, priority is the more relevant comparison.
What Priority Submetering Actually Means
Priority submetering is a contracted operating model, not a hardware SKU.

The meters may be similar to those used in a conventional project. The difference lies in who owns the equipment, who coordinates the work, who administers billing, and who remains accountable after installation.

Standard submetering often leaves the owner with a collection of components and decisions. The owner may purchase equipment, coordinate installers, arrange data collection, select billing software, and manage resident questions. Priority service packages those responsibilities into a provider-led programme. Think of standard submetering as buying a security camera and arranging the wiring yourself. Priority submetering is hiring a monitored service that owns the camera, manages the wiring, watches the alerts, and maintains the response process.
For broader context on how property technology affects building operations,
insights from Access Management Group
can help owners place submetering within a wider technology strategy.
The accountability difference
A priority provider typically takes responsibility for:
Meter specification:
Selecting equipment suited to the utility, building layout, and jurisdiction.
Field delivery:
Coordinating installation crews, access requirements, commissioning, and corrections.
Utility coordination:
Confirming interfaces, service requirements, and project dependencies.
Billing administration:
Converting validated readings into regulated, itemised sub-bills where permitted.
Compliance support:
Preparing the technical and operational documentation required by the applicable rules.
Ongoing service:
Monitoring system performance, maintaining equipment, and managing replacements under the agreement.

The owner still has important duties. Suite access must be organised. Residents need timely notices. Property staff should appoint one informed contact who can make decisions and resolve site issues quickly. Priority doesn't eliminate owner participation. It removes the need for the owner to act as the meter manufacturer, project manager, billing operator, and service department.

The Four Core Value Propositions

Priority service has four practical value propositions, but they shouldn't be treated as four unrelated features. Cost recovery, leak control, billing quality, and compliance reinforce one another. A meter that produces data without a billing process is incomplete. A billing process without verified measurements creates risk. A leak alert without someone responsible for responding is just another notification.

children.text: Cost recovery starts with measured responsibility

Unit-level measurement gives the owner a defensible basis for assigning consumption where the governing rules permit it. It also gives residents a visible reason to change usage. In Ontario, the University of Toronto study estimated an electricity-use reduction of
about 20% after sub-metering
, as recorded in the
Ontario condominium sub-metering study
. That result matters because the financial return isn't limited to passing through an expense. The property can also reduce purchased consumption when occupants see the cost of their own behaviour.
Leak detection protects more than the water budget

A priority scope should specify leak and flood detection, alert routing, escalation, and responsibility for reviewing exceptions. The system should distinguish a normal consumption pattern from a persistent flow, a sudden spike, or an abnormal common-area event. The owner doesn't need a dashboard that merely displays yesterday's problem. They need a process that identifies unusual activity early enough for staff or a contractor to investigate.
Tenant billing creates an audit trail

Automated billing can replace spreadsheets, manual reads, and repeated reconciliation between utility invoices and resident accounts. It should show the meter reading, billing period, applicable rate or allocation rule, adjustments, and account history. That record gives property staff a consistent answer when a resident, board member, lender, or auditor asks how a charge was calculated.
Compliance is a design requirement
In Ontario, a licensed unit sub-metering provider must meet
Measurement Canada standards as the minimum installation and measurement standard
. The Ontario Energy Board's Unit Sub-Metering Code also establishes minimum conditions and standards for licensed providers serving a master consumer, according to the
Ontario sub-metering compliance report

That means compliance must be built into meter selection, installation, commissioning, data controls, and billing. It can't be added after the first invoice. Ontario regulations also state that unit sub-meter providers aren't generally required to interface with the provincial smart meter data repository unless a code or order requires it. Owners should therefore ask how the provider verifies readings and reconciles billing without assuming utility-style data access. The
Ontario regulation on unit sub-metering providers
is particularly relevant to that question.
Practical rule:
Ask the provider to demonstrate the complete chain from meter reading to resident invoice, including exception handling and verification records.

The four propositions compound. Recovered utility expense supports the service economics. Leak monitoring reduces avoidable loss and damage exposure. Billing records improve resident communication. Compliance controls make the entire operating model defensible.
How a Priority Deployment Unfolds
A priority deployment should run on a visible critical path, not a vague promise that installation will happen quickly. A typical Axis Meter Solutions programme targets
8 to 10 weeks from agreement to live meters

, including equipment lead time, as described in the company's service information. The exact schedule still depends on access, building conditions, jurisdictional requirements, and the owner's responsiveness.

children.text: Six stages from agreement to revenue readiness
Agreement and kickoff:
The parties define the building scope, service terms, billing model, utility coverage, responsibilities, and approval path.
Site survey:
The project team reviews utility drawings, meter locations, panel access, communication conditions, pipework, suite access, and resident-notice requirements.
Engineering plan:
The provider specifies meters, sensors, communication equipment, installation methods, data architecture, and commissioning tests.
Parallel procurement and mobilisation:
Equipment reservations, crew planning, documentation, and utility coordination proceed together rather than waiting for each task to finish in sequence.
Installation and commissioning:
Crews install meters and included sensors, configure the network, register endpoints, and test consumption capture at each location.
Soft launch and dashboard activation:
Staff receive portal training, exception reports, and resident notice templates. The provider validates data, corrects gaps, and activates billing only after the acceptance checks pass.

The distinction between “installed” and “revenue-ready” is critical. A meter can be physically mounted while its endpoint remains unregistered, its suite assignment is wrong, or its reading has not passed validation. Require a unit-level status report that identifies installation, connectivity, data validation, billing readiness, and outstanding exceptions separately.

The owner should receive weekly updates covering completed locations, blocked access, open technical issues, resident communications, billing readiness, and decisions required. This turns speed into something measurable. It also gives the owner an early warning when a site condition threatens the launch date.

Turning Priority Submetering Into Measurable Returns

Owners should present priority submetering in the same language they use for every other operating decision. The board doesn't need a catalogue of meters. It needs a clear connection between the contract and the financial outcome.
Start with the
NOI line
. Recoverable utility charges can reduce the expense burden or create a more transparent pass-through structure where permitted. Next, show the
capital treatment

. Provider-owned equipment under a zero-upfront structure can preserve owner capital, but the service fee and agreement obligations must appear clearly in the forecast. Then quantify administrative impact through fewer manual reads, standardised invoices, exception reports, and a defined resident-support workflow.
An owner should also separate three return categories:
Recurring recovery:
Charges supported by validated consumption and applicable billing rules.
Avoided loss:
Water or energy waste identified through alerts and corrected through maintenance.
Risk reduction:
Better records, controlled billing, documented commissioning, and clearer responsibility for service failures.

The Ontario evidence supports treating conservation as part of the financial model. A 2016 Ontario impact analysis found that switching from bulk metering to sub-metering reduced electricity use by an average of
139 kWh per unit per month in the first year
, equivalent to a
40% reduction
. The same analysis estimated potential province-wide savings of
over 1 TWh annually
after full deployment across eligible bulk-metered buildings and a summer peak-demand reduction of
158 MW
, as reported in the
Ontario Energy Board Unit Sub-Metering Code material
Use the
NOI guidance for property owners

to translate the recovery model into the terms used by lenders and investors. Keep the calculation transparent. Don't count gross billing as net benefit until service charges, vacancy, bad debt, maintenance, and legal recoverability are included.
Verification checklist before signing
Confirm licensing:
Verify that the provider holds the required licence in the operating jurisdiction.
Review the leak SLA:
Identify who receives alerts, how quickly they respond, and what happens after an escalation.
Validate data cadence:
Confirm reading frequency, exception reporting, retention, corrections, and billing cut-off procedures.
Test the invoice trail:
Ask for a sample bill linked back to meter data and the applicable calculation.
Check building references:
Request references from properties with a similar utility layout, occupancy model, and billing complexity.
Define acceptance:
Put installation, commissioning, data validation, billing readiness, and unresolved defects into the contract.

Priority submetering earns approval when the owner can connect each service commitment to a measurable operating result. If the property reduces purchased water by 8%, the assumed annual saving is $14,400. Over seven years, that produces $100,800 before service costs and any allocation of savings.

The same scenario assumes billing recoveries of $6 per unit per month, producing $8,640 annually. Gross annual recovery therefore reaches $23,040 under the stated assumptions. The owner still needs to subtract the provider's service charge, confirm that billing is legally recoverable, and test whether the assumed reduction reflects the building's actual consumption profile.

Scenario two, a mixed-use tower approaching opening

Assume a new 180-unit mixed-use tower requires tenant billing at opening. The priority programme avoids a two-month delay in meter activation, allowing the owner to begin recovering eligible utility costs sooner. If 80% of units are occupied and each billed unit generates a $45 monthly utility recovery, the assumed gross recovery is $5,400 per month, or $64,800 annually.

The value here isn't only the annual figure. Timing matters. A provider that bundles equipment, installation, billing administration, and leak monitoring into a monthly service can let the owner align the cost with operating revenue rather than fund the entire installation before occupancy.

Scenario Key Assumptions Gross Annual Recovery Net Benefit and Payback
120-suite mid-rise condominium $180,000 annual water and sewer cost, 8% reduction, $6 monthly recovery per unit $23,040 Gross recovery less service costs; payback depends on the contracted fee and eligible billing rules
180-unit mixed-use tower 80% occupancy, $45 monthly recovery per billed unit, billing active at opening $64,800 Gross recovery less service costs; earlier activation improves timing but doesn't guarantee payback

For additional context on how providers present project outcomes, review the Axis Meter Solutions case studies. Don't treat any example as a substitute for a building-specific model. Local rules, vacancy, consumption patterns, service fees, meter coverage, and resident recoverability determine the actual result.

The board package should show separate rows for gross annual recovery, implementation or service cost, net cash flow, and payback period. If those rows aren't available, the proposal is still a product pitch rather than an investment analysis.

Turning Priority Submetering Into Measurable Returns

Owners should present priority submetering in the same language they use for every other operating decision. The board doesn't need a catalogue of meters. It needs a clear connection between the contract and the financial outcome.

Start with the NOI line. Recoverable utility charges can reduce the expense burden or create a more transparent pass-through structure where permitted. Next, show the capital treatment. Provider-owned equipment under a zero-upfront structure can preserve owner capital, but the service fee and agreement obligations must appear clearly in the forecast. Then quantify administrative impact through fewer manual reads, standardised invoices, exception reports, and a defined resident-support workflow.

An owner should also separate three return categories:

  • Recurring recovery: Charges supported by validated consumption and applicable billing rules.
  • Avoided loss: Water or energy waste identified through alerts and corrected through maintenance.
  • Risk reduction: Better records, controlled billing, documented commissioning, and clearer responsibility for service failures.

The Ontario evidence supports treating conservation as part of the financial model. A 2016 Ontario impact analysis found that switching from bulk metering to sub-metering reduced electricity use by an average of 139 kWh per unit per month in the first year, equivalent to a 40% reduction. The same analysis estimated potential province-wide savings of over 1 TWh annually after full deployment across eligible bulk-metered buildings and a summer peak-demand reduction of 158 MW, as reported in the Ontario Energy Board Unit Sub-Metering Code material.

Use the NOI guidance for property owners to translate the recovery model into the terms used by lenders and investors. Keep the calculation transparent. Don't count gross billing as net benefit until service charges, vacancy, bad debt, maintenance, and legal recoverability are included.

Verification checklist before signing

  • Confirm licensing: Verify that the provider holds the required licence in the operating jurisdiction.
  • Review the leak SLA: Identify who receives alerts, how quickly they respond, and what happens after an escalation.
  • Validate data cadence: Confirm reading frequency, exception reporting, retention, corrections, and billing cut-off procedures.
  • Test the invoice trail: Ask for a sample bill linked back to meter data and the applicable calculation.
  • Check building references: Request references from properties with a similar utility layout, occupancy model, and billing complexity.
  • Define acceptance: Put installation, commissioning, data validation, billing readiness, and unresolved defects into the contract.

Priority submetering earns approval when the owner can connect each service commitment to a measurable operating result.
